source_batch.unit_label: BRBL Module B unit 2: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Assess payment in due course using apparent tenor, good faith, care and entitlement warning signs

facts.statement: Payment in due course requires payment according to apparent tenor, in good faith and without negligence, to a person in possession where circumstances supply no reasonable ground to believe that person lacks entitlement to payment.
facts.locator: S04 printed pp. 156–157; PDF page = printed page + 19

facts.statement: Payment in due course requires payment according to apparent tenor, in good faith and without negligence, to a person in possession where circumstances supply no reasonable ground to believe that person lacks entitlement to payment.

payload.title: Payment in due course is a combined test
payload.core_explanation_md:
A bank should not reduce **payment in due course** to one successful check. Section 10 combines the instrument's apparent terms, good faith, absence of negligence and circumstances that do not reasonably suggest the recipient is not entitled. Possession is relevant, but it is not the entire test.

Consider a payment file with a clean-looking image but an unresolved warning about the presenter's entitlement. The clean image addresses only part of the decision. The bank still needs to deal with the warning; a favourable result on one condition cannot substitute for the others.

self_check.prompt_text: Can good faith alone establish payment in due course?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Apparent tenor, care and the circumstances of entitlement also matter.

payload.title: Investigate warning signs before relying on a payment defence
payload.core_explanation_md:
The practical question is what a careful payment decision should have noticed from the instrument and surrounding circumstances. A mismatch with the visible payment date, an unresolved instruction affecting payment or a reasonable concern about entitlement needs attention before release.

This is not a promise that a banker must discover every concealed fraud. The learning task is to distinguish a hidden problem despite ordinary care from a warning that was available and ignored. The available evidence and the checks actually performed belong in the file.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does an ignored entitlement warning matter even where the presenter physically holds the cheque?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 10 requires circumstances without reasonable grounds to doubt entitlement; possession alone cannot satisfy that requirement.

payload.stem_md: A payment officer says, “The presenter has the original cheque, so payment in due course is established.” Which response correctly applies Section 10?

options.text_md: Possession is irrelevant in every payment
options.explanation_md: The definition does refer to possession, but combines it with several other conditions.

options.text_md: Only the date printed on the cheque matters
options.explanation_md: Apparent tenor matters, but so do good faith, absence of negligence and the entitlement circumstances.

options.text_md: A clean signature eliminates every possible payment issue
options.explanation_md: A signature check alone does not resolve other terms or reasonable grounds to doubt entitlement.

options.text_md: Possession must be considered alongside tenor, good faith, care and entitlement circumstances
options.explanation_md: The statutory conditions work together; possession does not replace the remaining checks.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The statutory conditions work together; possession does not replace the remaining checks.

payload.stem_md: A branch intends to pay before the future date visible on a post-dated cheque. Which part of payment in due course is directly put in issue?

options.text_md: Only the recipient's occupation
options.explanation_md: Occupation does not answer whether payment follows the instrument's visible terms.

options.text_md: Payment according to the apparent tenor of the instrument
options.explanation_md: The visible payment date forms part of the terms the bank must respect.

options.text_md: Whether every indorsement was signed at the same branch
options.explanation_md: Branch location of signatures does not cure payment contrary to the cheque's visible date.

options.text_md: Whether the bank has a general policy of encouraging digital payments
options.explanation_md: A general digital-payment policy does not change the cheque's apparent terms.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The visible payment date forms part of the terms the bank must respect.

payload.stem_md: A bank pays honestly but ignores a readily visible defect that ordinary care would have addressed. Why is honesty alone insufficient for Section 10?

options.text_md: The definition requires the bank to guarantee discovery of all hidden fraud
options.explanation_md: Section 10 requires absence of negligence; that does not amount to a guarantee of discovering every concealed fraud.

options.text_md: Every payment must be personally approved by the drawer at the counter
options.explanation_md: The definition does not impose this universal counter-approval requirement.

options.text_md: Good faith and absence of negligence are separate requirements
options.explanation_md: An honest decision can still be negligent when available warning signs are ignored.

options.text_md: The recipient must always be the original payee in person
options.explanation_md: The definition is not confined to personal attendance by the original payee; entitlement circumstances must be assessed.

payload.correct_explanation_md: An honest decision can still be negligent when available warning signs are ignored.
